narr: In this section, we're going to dive deep into pointers in C programming.
Pointers are one of the most powerful features of C, but they can also be tricky to master.

data.heading: Function Pointers
bullets: Functions can modify caller variables using pointers
The ext_euclid function demonstrates this pattern
Pointers allow functions to return multiple values

narr: Let's start by looking at how functions can modify variables of the caller.
When we want a function to modify variables in the caller's scope, we pass pointers to those variables.
For example, the extended Euclidean algorithm function ext_euclid takes pointers to x and y, allowing it to modify these values.
After calling g = ext_euclid(a, b, &x, &y), the function returns g as the greatest common divisor while setting x and y to the Bézout coefficients.

data.heading: Pointer Function Example

narr: Here's how we declare and use a function that modifies variables through pointers.
First, we declare the function ext_euclid which takes two integers and two pointers to integers.
Then we declare our variables x, y, and g.
Finally, we call the function, passing the addresses of x and y using the & operator.
The function will modify x and y and return the greatest common divisor in g.

data.heading: Classic Swap Function
bullets: Swap function exchanges values using pointers
Temporary variable stores one value during swap
Pointer dereferencing modifies original variables

narr: One of the classic examples of pointer usage is the swap function.
The swap function takes two pointers to integers and exchanges their values.
It uses a temporary variable to store one value while performing the swap.
By dereferencing the pointers with the * operator, we modify the original variables in the caller's scope.

data.heading: Swap Function Implementation

narr: Here's the implementation of the swap function.
We declare a function that takes two pointers to integers.
We create a temporary variable temp and store the value pointed to by x in it.
Then we assign the value pointed to by y to the location pointed to by x.
Finally, we assign the value from temp to the location pointed to by y.
When we call swap(&a, &b), the values of a and b are exchanged.

data.heading: Pointer Pitfalls
bullets: Returning pointers to local variables is dangerous
Local variables exist only in the function's stack frame
The pointer becomes invalid after the function returns

narr: Now, let's look at a common pitfall with pointers.
Returning a pointer to a local array is invalid because the local variable goes out of scope when the function returns.
The pointer becomes invalid after the function's stack frame disappears.
Compilers usually warn about this issue, but it's up to the programmer to avoid this mistake.

data.heading: Dangerous Pointer Return

narr: This example shows the dangerous pattern of returning a pointer to a local array.
The get_message function creates a local array msg.
Then it returns a pointer to this local array.
In main, we store this pointer in string and try to print it.
This is undefined behavior because msg no longer exists when get_message returns.
The string might print correctly, or it might contain garbage, or the program might crash.
Now let's explore how arrays work in C, focusing on their relationship with pointers.
We'll look at how primitive arrays are implemented, the sizeof operator, and address arithmetic.

data.heading: Arrays and Pointers
bullets: Primitive arrays are implemented as pointers to continuous memory
Array name behaves like a pointer to element 0
Unlike pointers, arrays cannot be reassigned

narr: In C, primitive arrays are implemented as a pointer to a block of continuous memory.
The array name behaves like a pointer to the first element - arr is equivalent to &arr[0].
However, unlike a pointer, an array name cannot be reassigned to point to a different location.

data.heading: Array and Pointer Relationship

narr: Here's how arrays and pointers work together.
We declare an integer array arr with 8 elements.
We can access the first element with arr[0].
We can also create a pointer pa and initialize it with arr, which is equivalent to &arr[0].

data.heading: The sizeof Operator
bullets: sizeof() returns size in bytes
For variables - size of the type
For arrays - size of the entire array

narr: The sizeof operator is used to determine the size of types or variables in bytes.
For primitive types and variables, sizeof returns the size of the type.
For primitive arrays, sizeof returns the size of the entire array, not the size of a pointer.

data.heading: sizeof Examples

narr: Let's look at some examples of sizeof.
The size of a char is 1 byte by definition.
The size of a double is typically 8 bytes on a 64-bit operating system.
An int array of 8 elements will take 32 bytes on a 64-bit system (4 bytes per int).
A long array of 5 elements will take 40 bytes on a 64-bit system (8 bytes per long).

data.heading: Array Length Macro
bullets: C doesn't track array length natively
We can create a macro to calculate array length
Uses sizeof to divide total size by element size

narr: C doesn't natively track the length of arrays.
However, we can create a macro to calculate the array length.
This macro uses sizeof to divide the total size of the array by the size of one element.
We need to handle the edge case of an empty array to avoid division by zero.
Here's the implementation of the array_length macro.
It checks if the array is empty first to avoid division by zero.
If not empty, it divides the total size of the array by the size of the first element.
This gives us the number of elements in the array.

data.heading: Address Arithmetic
bullets: Pointers support addition and subtraction
pa + i points to arr[i]
Address increases by i × size of data type

narr: Address arithmetic is a powerful feature of pointers in C.
You can add or subtract integers from pointers.
When you add i to a pointer pa, it points to the element i positions away.
The actual address value increases by i multiplied by the size of the data type.

data.heading: Address Arithmetic Example
data.problem: If arr[0] has address 100 (int), what is the address of arr[3]?

narr: Let's work through an example of address arithmetic.
Suppose we have an integer array where arr[0] has address 100.
Each integer takes 4 bytes in memory.
Moving 3 elements forward means we need to add 3 × 4 = 12 bytes to the address.
Starting from address 100, adding 12 gives us address 112.
So arr[3] has address 112.

data.heading: Pointer Type Conversion Example
data.problem: If char pc = (char*)pa;, when does (int*)(pc + i) == pa + 3?

steps.text: pc is a char pointer, so each increment moves by 1 byte
pa is an int pointer, so each increment moves by 4 bytes
To match pa + 3, we need to move 3 × 4 = 12 bytes
Since pc moves by 1 byte per increment, i must be 12

narr: Here's an interesting question about pointer type conversion.
Suppose we have an int pointer pa and we create a char pointer pc from it.
When we increment pc by i, it moves by i bytes.
When we increment pa by 3, it moves by 3 × 4 = 12 bytes (assuming 4-byte integers).
For (int*)(pc + i) to equal pa + 3, we need to move exactly 12 bytes.
Since pc moves by 1 byte per increment, i must be 12.
Now let's turn our attention to strings in C.
We'll explore how strings are stored and the standard library functions for working with them.

data.heading: String Representation
bullets: Strings are stored as character arrays
Terminated by a null byte (\0)
Work with strings as with arrays

narr: In C, strings are stored as arrays of characters.
They are terminated by a null byte (\0), which marks the end of the string.
We can work with strings just like we work with character arrays.

data.heading: String Manipulation

narr: Here's an example of how we can manipulate strings using pointer arithmetic.
We declare a string str and a character pointer pc initialized to str.
We can access individual characters using pointer notation - *(pc+10) accesses the 11th character.
Changing this character to 'S' modifies the original string.
When we print the string, it shows the modification: "This is a String."

data.heading: string.h Library Functions
bullets: Copying: strcpy(), strncpy()
Comparison: strcmp(), strncmp()
Length: strlen()
Concatenation: strcat(), strncat()
Character search: strchr(), strrchr()

narr: The C standard library provides a set of functions in string.h for working with strings.
These functions include copying, comparison, length calculation, concatenation, and character search.
Let's look at each of these categories in more detail.

data.heading: string.h Function Signatures
rows: Copies n characters from strfrom to strto
Compares str1 and str2: 0 if equal; positive if str1 > str2; negative if str1 < str2
Compares the first n characters of str1 and str2
Appends strfrom to the end of strto
Appends n characters from strfrom to the end of strto
Searches for character c in str: pointer to the first occurrence or NULL
Pointer to the last occurrence of c or NULL

narr: Here's a comprehensive list of the string.h functions and their signatures.
strcpy copies one string to another.
strncpy copies a specified number of characters from one string to another.
strcmp compares two strings and returns 0 if they're equal, a positive value if the first is greater, or a negative value if the first is smaller.
strncmp compares only the first n characters of two strings.
strlen returns the length of a string.
strcat appends one string to the end of another.
strncat appends a specified number of characters from one string to another.
strchr searches for the first occurrence of a character in a string and returns a pointer to it.
strrchr searches for the last occurrence of a character in a string.
Finally, let's look at some search and sort algorithms that make excellent use of pointers.
These algorithms demonstrate the power and efficiency that pointer manipulation can bring.

data.heading: Linear Search
bullets: Returns a pointer to the found element or NULL
Time complexity: O(n)
Simple but inefficient for large arrays

narr: Linear search is the simplest search algorithm.
It iterates through an array element by element, comparing each element to the target value.
If found, it returns a pointer to the element.
If not found after checking all elements, it returns NULL.
The time complexity is O(n), meaning it scales linearly with the size of the array.

data.heading: Linear Search Implementation

narr: Here's an implementation of linear search using pointers.
We take an integer value to search for in the array.
We initialize two pointers: parr to the start of the array and parrend to the end.
We iterate through the array using pointer arithmetic.
If we find the value, we immediately return a pointer to that element.
If we finish the loop without finding the value, we return NULL.

data.heading: Insertion Sort
bullets: Time complexity: O(n²)
Builds final sorted array one element at a time
Works well for small or nearly sorted arrays

narr: Insertion sort is another simple sorting algorithm.
It has a time complexity of O(n²), making it inefficient for large arrays.
The algorithm works by building the final sorted array one element at a time.
For each element, it finds the correct position in the sorted portion and inserts it there.
It performs well for small arrays or arrays that are already nearly sorted.

data.heading: Insertion Sort Implementation

narr: Here's an implementation of insertion sort split into two functions.
The shift_element function moves elements down to make space for insertion.
It starts with the value at position i and shifts previous elements down until it finds the correct position.
The insertion_sort function iterates through the array, calling shift_element whenever it finds an element out of order.
Together, these functions implement the insertion sort algorithm using pointer arithmetic.

data.heading: Quicksort
bullets: Time complexity: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) in worst case
Divide-and-conquer algorithm
Implemented in standard library as qsort()

narr: Quicksort is a more efficient sorting algorithm with an average time complexity of O(n log n).
However, it has a worst-case complexity of O(n²) when the array is already sorted or nearly sorted.
Quicksort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that works by selecting a 'pivot' element.
It partitions the array such that elements smaller than the pivot are on one side and larger elements are on the other.
Then it recursively sorts the two partitions.
The standard library provides an implementation of quicksort as the qsort function.

data.heading: Quicksort Implementation

narr: Here's the beginning of a quicksort implementation.
The function takes left and right indices to define the portion of the array to sort.
If left >= right, there's nothing to sort, so we return.
We select the pivot as the middle element and swap it with the leftmost element.
This places the pivot at the beginning of the array for easier partitioning.
The pivot value is stored in the variable pivot.

data.heading: Key Points
items: Pointers allow functions to modify caller variables
Arrays and pointers are closely related in C
Address arithmetic enables efficient array manipulation
string.h provides many useful string functions
Search and sort algorithms demonstrate pointer power

narr: Let's recap the key points we've covered in this section.
Pointers are a fundamental feature of C that allow functions to modify variables in the caller's scope.
Arrays and pointers are closely related in C, with array names behaving like pointers to the first element.
Address arithmetic enables efficient manipulation of array elements through pointer operations.
The string.h library provides many useful functions for working with strings.
Search and sort algorithms demonstrate the power and efficiency that pointer manipulation can bring.
